rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq dates the siege to year five and says fifteen thousand confederates gathered; Mālik dates it to year four. The trench was dug at Salmān's suggestion.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فاجتمعوا خمسة عشر ألفا، وهم الأحزاب، ونزلوا المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Breaking an intractable rock was a great miracle: flashes showed the Prophet Persian, Byzantine, and Abyssinian cities and their coming conquest.
rows.anchor: وظهرت للرسول به تلك المعجزة العظيمة من كسر الصخرة التي أعوزت الصحابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The east wind wrecked enemy houses, extinguished fires, cut ropes, overturned pots, and made the besiegers unable to stay; angels strengthened the wind.
rows.anchor: بعث الله الصبا لنصرة نبيه، فأضرت بهم هدمت بيوتهم، وأطفأت نيرانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads وجنودا with fatḥa on jīm, the majority with ḍamma; Abū ʿAmr and Abū Bakra report a yāʾ reading of لم يروها, while the seven and majority use tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: وجنودا، بفتح الجيم والجمهور: بالضم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first interpretation places the above and below armies east and west in the valley; Mujāhid instead identifies Najd under ʿUyayna and Mecca with the rest of Tihāma.
rows.anchor: من فوقكم: من أعلى الوادي من قبل مشرق غطفان، ومن أسفل منكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view locates groups on Medina's upper and lower sides; Abū Ḥayyān says the views are close and the wording may hyperbolically depict encirclement.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما يراد ما يختص ببقعة المدينة، أي نزلت طائفة في أعلى المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaygh of the eyes is departure from a steady gaze, like the look of someone bewildered by terror; al-Farrāʾ says they looked only at the enemy.
rows.anchor: وزيغ الأبصار: ميلها عن مستوى نظرها، فعل الواله الجزع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearts reaching throats emphatically depicts agitation and pounding, not literal movement; other explanations say fear makes the pounding reach the throat or contracts the heart there.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يجد خشونة وقلبه يصعد علوا لينفصل، فالبلوغ ليس حقيقة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further explanations say fear blocks breathing or an inflated lung raises the heart; the passage cites another Qurʾānic image of hearts at throats.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يفضي إلى أن يسد مخرج النفس، فلا يقدر المرء أن يتنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الظنون is plural because expectations had different objects; despite disagreement about plural verbal nouns, Abū ʿAmr cites poetry using the plural form.
rows.anchor: والظنون: جمع لما اختلفت متعلقاته، وإن كان لا ينقاس عند من جمع المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr's al-Aghānī poem uses الظنونا as evidence for the plural.
rows.anchor: أنشد أبو عمرو في كتاب الألحان: إذا الجوزاء أردفت الثريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pure believers trusted the promised victory; weak believers wavered and hypocrites expected defeat, all included by the pronoun. Al-Ḥasan similarly distinguishes the hypocrites' expectation of destruction from believers' expectation of a test.
rows.anchor: فظن المؤمنون الخلص أن ما وعدهم الله من النصر حق

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says believers nearly wavered and wondered about a breach of promise; such passing thoughts cannot be warded off, unlike hypocrites' voiced claims.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: أي يكادون يضطربون، ويقولون: ما هذا الخلف للوعد؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ on the written alifs in الظنونا والرسولا والسبيلا; Abū ʿUbayd and expert readers prefer pausing with the written alif and not connecting it, preserving codex spelling and Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو عبيد والحذاق أن يوقف على هذه الكلمة بالألف، ولا يوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: هنالك is a distant-place adverb for the siege and fighting, governed by ابتلي; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a time adverb, which Abū Ḥayyān finds weak if governed by وتظنون.
rows.anchor: وهنالك: ظرف مكان للبعيد هذا أصله، فيحمل عليه، أي في ذلك المكان

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the test was hunger; Mujāhid says siege, and another view says steadfastness in faith.
rows.anchor: وابتلاؤهم، قال الضحاك: بالجوع. وقال مجاهد: بالحصار.

rows.speaker: ابن سلام
rows.claim: Ibn Sallām says زلزلوا means moved by fear; other views say they remained firm or were moved toward temptation but protected.
rows.anchor: وزلزلوا، قال ابن سلام: حركوا بالخوف. وقيل زلزلوا، فثبتوا وصبروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read زلزلوا with ḍamma; a report from Abū ʿAmr has kasra, with another report describing an imāla-like coloring. Most read زلزالا with kasra, while al-Jaḥdarī and ʿĪsā use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وزلزلوا، بضم الزاي. وقرأ أحمد بن موسى اللؤلؤي، عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites display faith and conceal unbelief; people whose hearts are sick are weak believers, distinct from hypocrites in the coordinated phrase.
rows.anchor: وإذ يقول المنافقون: وهم المظهرون للإيمان المبطنون الكفر. والذين في قلوبهم مرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After flashes and promises of conquering Persia, Byzantium, Mecca, and Abyssinia, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr mocked the promise because they could barely relieve themselves.
rows.anchor: قال معتب بن قشير: يعدنا محمد أن نفتح كنوز كسرى وقيصر ومكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God's and His Messenger's promise deception was mockery, showing they did not believe him a real Messenger; the verse concerns Muʿattib and his counterparts.
rows.anchor: وقولهم: ما وعدنا الله ورسوله إلا غرورا، هو على سبيل الهزء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faction of hypocrites said there was no secure place in battle and urged people home; another view says they called them back to unbelief. Al-Suddī names ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and companions, Muqātil Banū Salima, Aws ibn Rumān Aws ibn Qubṭī and companions, al-Kalbī Banū Ḥāritha; Abū Ḥayyān allows these reports all true.
rows.anchor: لا مقام لكم في حومة القتال والممانعة، فارجعوا إلى بيوتكم ومنازلكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For لا مقام لكم, one set reads mīm with ḍamma and the rest with fatḥa; both readings can mean a place or the act of standing.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السلمي والأعرج واليماني وحفص: بضم الميم، فاحتمل أن يكون مكانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The permission-seeker is identified as Aws ibn Qubṭī, who sought to enter Medina with his clan's agreement; he claimed the homes were exposed to attack or empty for thieves.
rows.anchor: ويستأذن فريق منهم النبي: هو أوس بن قبطي، استأذن في الدخول إلى المدينة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows عورة as a lightened form or active participle; Ibn Jinnī says wāw remains sound because it is vowelled after fatḥa, and Abū Ḥayyān explains the expected alif conversion.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جني: صحة الواو في هذا إشارة لأنها متحركة قبلها فتحة.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the homes were empty of men; Qatāda calls them remote and feared for the enemy; al-Suddī says low walls made them vulnerable to thieves; al-Layth defines ʿawra as nakedness or anything shameful.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: عورة: خالية من الرجال ضائعة. وقال قتادة: قاصية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Jews urged ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and the hypocrites back to Medina, claiming safety; Abū Ḥayyān says this hid flight.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: قالت اليهود لعبد الله ابن أبي ابن سلول وأصحابه من المنافقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in دخلت most naturally refers to the houses but could mean Medina or their families; the requested fitna means apostasy and open unbelief, or fighting Muslims.
rows.anchor: والضمير في: دخلت، الظاهر عوده على البيوت، إذ هو أقرب مذكور.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read لآتوها short, meaning come to the fitna; the other seven lengthen it, meaning give in to it.
rows.anchor: لآتوها: أي لجاءوا إليها وفعلوا على قراءة القصر، وهي قراءة نافع وابن كثير.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says that if the enemies entered and battle intensified, hypocrites would hasten to fight Muḥammad, staying home only long enough to seize weapons.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ولو دخلت المدينة من أقطارها، واشتد الحرب الحقيقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read سئلوا; al-Ḥasan reads سولوا, and other reports alter hamza or its vowel through dialect or sound change.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: سئلوا، وقرأ الحسن: سولوا، بواو ساكنة بعد السين المضمومة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the fitna was fighting for tribal partisanship; al-Ḥasan says shirk, and Abū Ḥayyān says the pronoun most plainly refers to fitna.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: ثم سئلوا الفتنة: أي القتال في العصبية، لأسرعوا إليه.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan interprets the fitna as shirk; Abū Ḥayyān says the pronoun most plainly refers to fitna, though another view refers it to Medina.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الفتنة، الشرك، والظاهر عود الضمير بها على الفتنة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pledge acts like an oath answered by لا يولون; the answer shifts to third person for meaning. Banū Ḥāritha and Banū Salima had faltered at Uḥud then vowed not to flee; another report locates the covenant at the ʿAqaba or among men absent from Badr.
rows.anchor: وعاهدوا: أجري مجرى اليمين، ولذلك يتلقى بقوله: لا يولون الأدبار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke says flight cannot escape God's decree; their remaining lifespan is short. The conditional answer is omitted because the preceding clause supplies it.
rows.anchor: قل لن ينفعكم الفرار: خطاب توبيخ وإعلام أن الفرار لا ينجي من القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قليلا may qualify omitted enjoyment or a period of time; when وإذا follows a conjunction it need not govern, explaining a cited reading in al-Isrāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقليلا: نعت لمصدر محذوف، أي تمتيعا قليلا، أو لزمان محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Marwānid hurried past a leaning wall when this verse was recited to him and replied that the short time was what they sought.
rows.anchor: ومر بعض المروانية على حائط مائل فأسرع، فتليت له هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: من ذا is a rhetorical question carrying negation: no one can protect them from God.
rows.anchor: ومن ذا: استفهام، ركبت ذا مع من وفيه معنى النفي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains paired mercy and harm as harm if God wills mercy, or as prevention from God's intention; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the first for needless ellipsis and accepts the second.
rows.anchor: أما الوجه الأول ففيه حذف جملة لا ضرورة تدعو إلى حذفها، والثاني هو الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites discouraged Medinan Anṣār from aiding the Prophet, saying Muḥammad and his companions were only a morsel that Abū Sufyān would devour; another view says Jews invited them to join.
rows.anchor: والقائلين لإخوانهم كانوا، أي المنافقون، يثبطون إخوانهم من ساكني المدينة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd tells of a man who found his brother eating and drinking while the Prophet faced battle; the brother predicted defeat, the man denounced him, and Gabriel brought the verse.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: انصرف رجل من عند رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، يوم الأحزاب

rows.speaker: ابن السائب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sāʾib says the verse concerns ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr and retreating hypocrites, who told people to stay and summoned allies back.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن السائب: هي في عبد الله بن أبي، ومعتب بن قشير، ومن رجع من المنافقين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls هلموا إلينا a transitive verb meaning bring yourselves near; Abū Ḥayyān says grammarians treat هلم as a compound, either ها plus لم or هل plus أم, and as transitive or intransitive.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وهلموا إلينا، أي قربوا أنفسكم إلينا، قال: وهو صوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites joined battle only briefly, under pressure and for show or public image, not genuine fighting.
rows.anchor: ولا يأتون البأس: أي القتال، إلا قليلا. يخرجون مع المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أشحة is an irregular plural; stinginess may concern lives, status, or wealth spent for God or booty, and Abū Ḥayyān prefers taking it broadly as all benefits to believers.
rows.anchor: ومتعلق الشح بأنفسهم، أو بأحوالهم، أو بأموالهم في النفقات في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says they cower in danger, then turn possessive when spoils are distributed; Abū Ḥayyān calls this an excessive loading of the wording.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أشحة عليكم في وقت الحرب، أضناء بكم، يترفرفون عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read أشحة accusative, parsed as blame or a circumstantial modifier of different clauses; Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads it nominative as an implied they are stingy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أشحة، بالنصب. قال الفراء: على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When fear comes, hypocrites cling to the Prophet with eyes circling like one fainting from death; the image's syntax allows it to modify circling or looking.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاء الخوف من العدو، وتوقع أن يستأصل أهل المدينة، لاذ هؤلاء المنافقون بك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they lash believers with their tongues or press for spoils; Yazīd ibn Rumān specifies verbal harm, insults and disparaging the law.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: بسطوا ألسنتهم فيكم. قال يزيد بن رومان: في أذى المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views say their speech asks insistently for booty or flatters believers to manipulate them; most read سلقوكم with sīn, Ibn Abī ʿAbla with ṣād.
rows.anchor: وقيل: السلق في مخادعة المؤمنين بما يرضيهم من القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second أشحة may be nominative or accusative and may refer to stinginess over booty, their own wealth, or the Prophet's victory.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في هذا: أشحة على مال الغنائم. وقيل: على مالهم الذي ينفقونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites never had true faith and their works were void and unaccepted; their stinginess or gaze was insignificant and ineffective.
rows.anchor: أولئك لم يؤمنوا، إشارة إلى المنافقين: أي لم يكن لهم قط إيمان.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the passage teaches verbal profession alone is not faith and hypocrites' works are void; Abū Ḥayyān objects that عسى cannot complement من.
rows.anchor: قلت: لا، ولكن تعليم لمن عسى يظن أن الإيمان باللسان إيمان

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd, from his father, says a man who fought at Badr later became a hypocrite and had his deeds invalidated.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد، عن أبيه: نزلت في رجل بدري، نافق بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites wished they had stayed among nomadic tent-dwellers, learning of the battle by asking travelers rather than seeing it; if present they would fight little for show.
rows.anchor: تمنوا لخوفهم بما منوا به عند الكرة أنهم مقيمون في البدو مع الأعراب

rows.speaker: ابن السائب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sāʾib says their only combat was throwing stones; readers vary forms of بادون and the verb for asking.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السائب: رميا بالحجارة خاصة دون سائر أنواع القتال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read يسألون; an unhamzated attribution to Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim is unknown to Abū Ḥayyān, while others read that people ask one another.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يسئلون، مضارع سأل. وحكى ابن عطية أن أبا عمرو وعاصما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to believers, not hypocrites; the Prophet is their example, and they owe him support because he fought beside them and endured injury, loss of his uncle, and other harm.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الخطاب في قوله: لقد كان لكم، للمؤمنين، لقوله قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must aid and risk themselves for the Prophet; guidance to Islam is a greater benefit than their service and struggle.
rows.anchor: يجب عليكم أن تنصروه وتوازروه، ولا ترغبوا بأنفسكم عن نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: اليوم الآخر means Resurrection Day; أسوة is the predicate noun and several attachments are possible. Most read إسوة with kasra, ʿĀṣim with ḍamma; الرجاء means hope or fear.
rows.anchor: واليوم الآخر: يوم القيامة. وقيل: يوم السياق. وأسوة: اسم كان، ولكم: الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses لمن كان يرجوا as apposition to لكم; Abū Ḥayyān says most Basrans reject apposition from an addressee pronoun, though Kufans and al-Akhfash allow it.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: بدل من لكم، كقوله: للذين استضعفوا لمن آمن منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise may refer to the test before Paradise or the Prophet's warning while digging the trench that the confederates would arrive and believers prevail; they accepted the trial and awaited its end.
rows.anchor: وكان الله وعدهم أن يزلزلهم حتى يستنصروه في قوله: أم حسبتم أن تدخلوا الجنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet told companions the confederates would arrive in nine or ten nights; seeing them approach confirmed the promise.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس، قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، لأصحابه: «إن الأحزاب سائرون إليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The increase was in what they believed—the promised events—not in faith's essence; Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads an added wāw in وما زادوهم, referring to the confederates.
rows.anchor: فالزيادة فيما يؤمن، لا في نفس الإيمان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صدقوا ما عاهدوا may have a dropped preposition, or صدق may take one object and metaphorically treat the covenant as one to whom they were true.
rows.anchor: فما عاهدوا، إما أن يكون على إسقاط الحرف، أي فيما عاهدوا

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Muqātil and al-Kalbī say the covenant-keepers were the seventy people of the ʿAqaba pledge; Anas says men who missed Badr vowed not to lag behind the Prophet, and Zayd ibn Rumān identifies Banū Ḥāritha.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل والكلبي: هم أهل العقبة السبعون، أهل البيعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قضى نحبه is figurative because death is inevitable; Mujāhid glosses it as the covenant, Abū ʿUbayda as a vow, and al-Zamakhsharī allows martyrdom or fulfilling the vow to stand firm.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من قضى نحبه، وهذا تجوز، لأن الموت أمر لا بد منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group says the phrase describes companions who fulfilled Islam's covenants completely, including martyrs and some of the ten promised Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: الموصوفون بقضاء النحب جماعة من الصحابة وفوا بعهود الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked on the pulpit who had fulfilled his vow, the Prophet pointed to Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh; Ṭalḥa stood at Uḥud until his hand was injured and the Prophet said he earned Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقد سئل من الذي قضى نحبه وهو على المنبر؟ فدخل طلحة بن عبيد الله

rows.speaker: مجاهِد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the one waiting awaits a jihad day to fulfill his vow; depending on the first phrase's meaning, he awaits martyrdom or the highest rank of faith.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ينتظر يوما فيه جهاد، فيقضي نحبه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither those martyred nor those still waiting changed the covenant, unlike hypocrites who fled.
rows.anchor: وما بدلوا: لا المستشهدون، ولا من ينتظر.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya resolves the will clause by ellipsis: persistence in hypocrisy leads to punishment, while repentance leads to mercy; either stated outcome implies its omitted counterpart.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عطية: تعذيب المنافقين ثمرته إدامتهم الإقامة على النفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya's ellipsis omits the cause of punishment but states its result and names forgiveness while omitting its result; Abū Ḥayyān calls this good concision.
rows.anchor: فحذف سبب التعذيب، وأثبت المسبب، وهو التعذيب. وأثبت سبب الرحمة والغفران

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says God punishes if hypocrites do not repent and accepts them if they do; Abū Ḥayyān rejects making punishment conditional because it is definitively willed.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويعذبهم إن شاء إذا لم يتوبوا، ويتوب عليهم إذا تابوا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in ليجزي is read as consequence or purpose and may attach to وما بدلوا; al-Zamakhsharī depicts both groups as seeking outcomes, and al-Suddī explains death in hypocrisy or repentance.
rows.anchor: واللام في ليجزي، قيل: لام الصيرورة وقيل: لام التعليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent the confederates away in anger without gain and brought believers home; Abū Ḥayyān rejects parsing لم ينالوا خيرا as a detached or explanatory clause.
rows.anchor: ورد الله الذين كفروا الأحزاب عن المدينة، والمؤمنين إلى بلادهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God spared a general battle by sending wind and angels. Another view describes ʿAlī killing ʿAmr in single combat and Nawfal ibn al-Ḥārith and other enemies killed at the trench.
rows.anchor: وكفى الله المؤمنين القتال، بإرسال الريح والجنود، وهم الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text lists Muslim dead in the trench battle, including Muʿādh, Anas ibn Aws, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sahl, al-Ṭufayl, Thaʿlaba, and Kaʿb ibn Zayd, who was hit by a stray arrow.
rows.anchor: معاذ، وأنس بن أوس بن عتيك، وعبد الله بن سهل، وأبو عمرو، وهم من بني عبد الأشهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh did not raid after the trench; God ended repeated warfare by defeating them later through His power and might.
rows.anchor: ولم تغز قريش المسلمين بعد الخندق، وكفى الله مداومة القتال وعودته

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports the siege delayed four prayers until night; after relief, the Prophet ordered Bilāl to call an iqāma for each and prayed them.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي سعيد الخدري: حبسنا يوم الخندق، فلم نصل الظهر، ولا العصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book who aided the confederates are generally Banū Qurayẓa; al-Ḥasan says Banū al-Naḍīr. Panic caused surrender, but the verse foregrounds it as the greater joy.
rows.anchor: وأنزل الذين ظاهروهم: أي أعانوا قريشا ومن معهم من الأحزاب من أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man who saw Dihya al-Kalbī on a white mule was told it was Gabriel shaking Qurayẓa's forts and casting terror into their hearts.
rows.anchor: وقال رجل: يا رسول الله، مر بنا دحية الكلبي على بغلة بيضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel ordered an immediate march; the Prophet said not to pray ʿAṣr before reaching Qurayẓa. Some prayed en route and others at night, and Abū Ḥayyān says both were correct; the siege lasted fifteen to twenty-five nights.
rows.anchor: جاء جبريل وقت الظهر فقال: إن الله يأمرك بالخروج إلى بني قريظة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A count says six hundred fighters and seven hundred captives. Yaḥyā ibn Akhṭab, who led the betrayal, stayed under Saʿd's judgment and said he did not regret opposing Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانوا ستمائة مقاتل وسبعمائة أسير. وجيء يحيي بن أخطب النضيري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One woman, Lubāba, was killed for dropping a millstone on Khallād ibn Suwayd; he was the only person killed in the siege, while Abū Sufyān ibn Muḥṣin died there; Qurayẓa fell in year five.
rows.anchor: وقتل من نسائهم امرأة، وهي لبابة امرأة الحكم القرظي، كانت قد طرحت الرحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary between second- and third-person forms in تقتلون وتأسرون and between kasra and ḍamma on sīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وتأسرون، بتاء الخطاب وكسر السين وأبو حيوة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أورثكم suggests transfer after former owners died and were removed; palms and fields are mentioned first because they are useful and strengthen Muslim military capacity.
rows.anchor: وأورثكم: فيه إشعار أنه انتقل إليهم ذلك بعد موت أولئك المقتولين

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says God announced the future lands had already been decreed; al-Ḥasan says Rome and Persia, Qatāda says Mecca, and Muqātil, Yazīd ibn Rumān, and Ibn Zayd say Khaybar.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: أخبر تعالى أن قد قضى بذلك. وقال الحسن: أراد الروم وفارس.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects limiting the promised lands to named places and calls the claim that they meant the people's women an exegetical innovation.
rows.anchor: ولا وجه لهذه التخصيصات، ومن بدع التفاسير أنه أراد نساءهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read تطؤوها with hamza; Zayd ibn ʿAlī omits it, explained by replacing hamza with alif and deleting the resulting consonant before wāw. The ending points to future conquests.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: تطؤوها، بهمزة مضمومة بعدها واو. وقرأ زيد بن علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's power over everything signals many future Muslim conquests; as He gave these lands, He can give others.
rows.anchor: وكان في ذلك إشارة إلى فتحه على المسلمين الفتوح الكثيرة، وأنه لا يستبعد ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The occasion was that the wives wanted more clothing and maintenance after the Prophet gained Qurayẓa and al-Naḍīr, comparing their hardship with Persian and Byzantine luxury.
rows.anchor: سبب نزولها أن أزواجه، صلى الله عليه وسلم، تغايرن وأردن زيادة في كسوة ونفقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet then had nine wives, who are named in the passage; another report says ten, including a Ḥimyarī woman.
rows.anchor: وأزواجه إذ ذاك تسع: عائشة بنت أبي بكر، وحفصة بنت عمر

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم الصيرفي
rows.claim: Al-Ṣayrafī says the Prophet chose the Hereafter over worldly kingship, then offered the choice to his wives to prove their agreement; all but the Ḥimyarī woman chose God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو القاسم الصيرفي: لما خير رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، بين ملك الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet let beloved ʿĀʾisha consult her parents before reciting the passage; she immediately chose God, His Messenger, and the Hereafter and asked him not to tell the other wives.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه قال لعائشة، وبدأ بها، وكانت أحبهن إليه: «إني ذاكر لك أمرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning is that the Prophet himself would provide for and divorce wives who wanted worldly adornment; their choice alone did not end marriage. Most jurists say choosing the husband is not divorce.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنهن إذا اخترن الحياة الدنيا وزينتها، متعهن رسول الله وطلقهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Legal views differ: ʿAlī reports one revocable divorce; Ḥanafīs one irrevocable; al-Shāfiʿī one revocable alongside ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd; Mālik three. Another view defers divorce until the Prophet chooses a gracious release, closer to Abū Ḥayyān's reading.
rows.anchor: وإن اختارت نفسها، وقعت طلقة بائنة عند أبي حنيفة وأصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wives' chief concern and demand were immersion in worldly life and its comforts and adornments.
rows.anchor: والمعنى في الآية: أنه كان عظيم همكن ومطلبكن التعمق في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فتعالين is compared with a parallel command in Āl ʿImrān; jurists differ whether divorce provision is obligatory or recommended, citing the command in al-Baqara for obligation.
rows.anchor: وتقدم الكلام في: فتعالين في قوله تعالى: فقل تعالوا ندع أبناءنا وأبناءكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A gracious release may mean leaving the home, praising the woman, or honorable convictions and conduct; most read أمتعكن doubled, Zayd ibn ʿAlī lightly.
rows.anchor: والتسريح الجميل إما في دون البيت، أو جميل الثناء، والمعتقد وحسن العشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أعد means prepared; the explicit المحسنات replaces a pronoun to emphasize the virtue earning the reward.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أعد: هيأ ويسر، وأوقع الظاهر موقع المضمر تنبيها على الوصف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥumayd al-Kharrāz reads أمتعكن وأسرحكن indicatively as a fresh statement; most use jussive verbs answering command or condition, with an allowed parenthesis.
rows.anchor: وقراءة حميد الخراز: أمتعكن وأسرحكن، بالرفع على الاستئناف والجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The manifest indecency means disobedience and corrupt marital conduct, not adultery, from which the Prophet is protected and which is concealed; their revelatory setting and status double accountability.
rows.anchor: ولا يتوهم أنها الزنا، لعصمة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary the form and voice of يضاعف; fatḥa on its verb makes العذاب nominative, kasra accusative. Abū ʿUbayda and Abū ʿAmr say two punishments are added, making three total.
rows.anchor: ومن فتح العين رفع العذاب، ومن كسرها نصبه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قنوت means obedience and humble service to God in agreement with the Messenger.
rows.anchor: ومن يقنت: أي يطع ويخضع بالعبودية لله، وبالموافقة لرسوله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary gender agreement in يقنت and تعمل; some grammarians call masculine agreement weak, but Abū Ḥayyān cites a Qurʾānic parallel against that argument.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ومن يقنت بالمذكر، حملا على لفظ من، وتعمل بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الرزق الكريم means Paradise; Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows worldly provision, while Abū Ḥayyān calls weak the view that both doubled reward and punishment refer to this world and the next.
rows.anchor: والرزق الكريم: الجنة. قال ابن عطية: ويجوز أن يكون في ذلك وعد دنياوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their doubled reward is for seeking the Prophet's pleasure with good character, kind marital conduct, contentment, and devotion.
rows.anchor: وإنما ضوعف أجرهن لطلبهن رضا رسول الله، بحسن الخلق وطيب المعاشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wives differ from women of their age as Mothers of Believers and spouses of the best Messenger, with revelation descending in their homes.
rows.anchor: وهو كونكن أمهات المؤمنين وزوجات خير المرسلين. ونزل القرآن فيكن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī derives أحد from وحد and says no single group of women equals the wives; Abū Ḥayyān accepts the etymology but rejects the group sense and says أحد differs from واحد in root and meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أحد في الأصل بمعنى وحد، وهو الواحد ثم وضع في النفي العام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لستن كأحد means each individual wife is unlike an individual woman, not that the wives collectively are unmatched by groups of women.
rows.anchor: وقلنا: إن معنى كأحد: كشخص واحد، فأبقينا أحدا على موضوعه من التذكير

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads إن اتقيتن as if the wives seek or already possess piety, with فلا تخضعن answering the condition.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: إن اتقيتن: إن أردتن التقوى، وإن كن متقيات.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers the known sense of اتقى as encountering: if they meet someone they should not soften their speech, so virtue is not conditional.
rows.anchor: وعندي أنه محمول على أن معناه: إن استقبلتن أحدا، فلا تخضعن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān cites al-Nābigha's following line to support the sense encounter, although the quotation itself continues into the next page segment.
rows.anchor: وعندي أنه محمول على أن معناه: إن استقبلتن أحدا، فلا تخضعن.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says not to speak leniently; al-Ḥasan says not indecently, al-Kalbī says not to say what a suspicious man desires, and Ibn Zayd calls soft speech flirtation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لا ترخصن بالقول. وقال الحسن: لا تكلمن بالرفث.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech should be good and free of suggestive softness that forms an attachment; women must avoid the coy, gentle voice associated with prostitutes.
rows.anchor: أمر تعالى أن يكون الكلام خيرا، لا على وجه يظهر في القلب علاقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read فيطمع subjunctively after the prohibition; some use jussive, separately forbidding the man to desire. Abū Ḥayyān prefers subjunctive as showing soft speech causes desire.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فيطمع، بفتح الميم ونصب العين، جوابا للنهي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says sickness of heart is hypocrisy; ʿIkrima says sexual immorality or flirtation.
rows.anchor: والمرض، قال قتادة: النفاق وقال عكرمة: الفسق والغزل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قولا معروفا means speech neither sacred law nor sound reason rejects.
rows.anchor: وقلن قولا معروفا: والمحرم، وهو الذي لا تنكره الشريعة ولا العقول.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a woman among unrelated men should speak firmly without raising her voice; other glosses include sound speech without vulgarity, forceful or permitted speech, remembrance or needed conversation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: المرأة تندب إذا خالطت الأجانب، عليها بالمصاهرة إلى الغلظة

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha's line says the woman faced them with her hand, supporting the author’s meaning of اتقى as meet.
rows.anchor: سقط النصيف ولم ترد إسقاطه ... فتناولته واتقتنا باليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read وقرن with kasra from a verb meaning remain settled; Abū al-Fatḥ al-Hamadhānī proposes an origin meaning gather together, from قار يقار and قارة.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وقرن، بكسر القاف، من وقر يقر إذا سكن

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح الهمداني
rows.claim: Abū al-Fatḥ al-Hamadhānī relates the imperative to gathering oneself, from قار يقار and قارة for a group.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو الفتح الهمداني، في كتاب التبيان، وجها آخر قال: قار يقار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order is to remain at home and avoid adornment; ʿĀʾisha wept remembering her departure in the Camel conflict, and Sawda declined pilgrimage because God commanded her to remain.
rows.anchor: أمرهن تعالى بملازمة بيوتهن، ونهاهن عن التبرج، وأعلم تعالى أنه فعل الجاهلية

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda define tabarruj as strutting, coquettishness, and affected sway; Muqātil says veiling without fastening the scarf; al-Mubarrad says showing beauty that must be covered.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد وقتادة: التبرج: التبختر والتغنج والتكسر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الجاهلية الأولى implies earlier and later ignorance; exegetes offer competing chronologies from the sons of Adam to periods between prophets, including Noah, Abraham, David, Jesus and Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: والجاهلية الأولى: يدل على أن ثم جاهلية متقدمة وأخرى متأخرة.

rows.speaker: عكرمة والحكم بن عيينة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Ḥakam place it between Adam and Noah; Ibn ʿAbbās also says between Idrīs and Noah, when women had a husband and a lover.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة والحكم بن عيينة: ما بين آدم ونوح، وهي ثمانمائة سنة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī places it between Noah and Abraham; Muqātil also dates a kind of display to Nimrod's era, and al-Zamakhsharī to Abraham's birth.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي وغيره: ما بين نوح وإبراهيم. قال مقاتل: زمن نمروذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya places it in David and Solomon's time; al-Mubarrad describes sexual access divided between husband and lover; other views put it between Moses and Jesus or Jesus and Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: زمن داود وسليمان، كان للمرأة قميص من الدر
